summary: Defines the NULL encryption algorithm, which does nothing to the data, and explains its use with IPsec's ESP. This lets ESP provide authentication and integrity without hiding the contents. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: It is like a locked envelope that is made of clear glass. You still get the seal that proves nobody tampered with it, but the message is not hidden.

questions: what is null encryption in ipsec
can esp be used without encryption
what is the null encryption algorithm
how does esp work without encryption
is esp null as secure as ah
subtitle: A cipher that does nothing on purpose, so IPsec ESP can authenticate packets without hiding them.

tldr.problem: IPsec's Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) has optional encryption, but implementations needed a defined way to say 'no encryption' so that peers interoperate when only authentication and integrity are wanted.
tldr.mechanism: The NULL algorithm is the identity function: the output block equals the input block. Used inside ESP with a zero-bit key and a zero-bit IV, it stands for 'encryption not applied'.
tldr.outcome: ESP can provide authentication and integrity without confidentiality. NULL itself offers no security service at all.

today: RFC 2410 is a Proposed Standard, published in November 1998, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is meant to be read with the ESP specification in RFC 2406 and the roadmap in RFC 2411.

sections.title: Why a Do-Nothing Cipher
sections.content:
RFC 2410 defines the NULL encryption algorithm and its use with the IPsec Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP). ESP specifies an optional encryption algorithm for confidentiality and an optional authentication algorithm for authentication and integrity. NULL is a convenient way to represent the option of not applying encryption. The IPsec Domain of Interpretation document calls this ESP_NULL.

The introduction also tells a tongue-in-cheek story about NULL being a block cipher from Roman times. It is a joke; the technical content starts at the algorithm definition.
sections.eli5: Sometimes you want to prove a note was not changed, but you do not need to hide it. NULL is the pretend lock that lets the rules say so.

sections.title: The NULL Algorithm
sections.content:
NULL is defined with the identity function I applied to a block of data b: NULL(b) = I(b) = b. The data comes out exactly as it went in.

Because the algorithm is stateless, no IV or other cryptographic synchronization data needs to be sent, not per packet and not per SA. NULL has a block size of 1 byte, so padding is not necessary. The RFC says NULL can accept keys of varying lengths like other ciphers, but longer keys give no measurable increase in security. It also states that NULL is significantly faster than other commonly used symmetric encryption algorithms.
sections.eli5: NULL hands back exactly what you gave it, like a photocopier that makes a perfect copy. It needs no secret code and no extra setup.

sections.title: ESP_NULL Operational Requirements
sections.content:
ESP_NULL is NULL used within ESP. The RFC fixes two parameters to help interoperability:

  • For IKE key extraction, the key size MUST be zero (0) bits. The RFC gives interoperability and avoiding potential export control problems as the reasons.
  • The IV size MUST be zero (0) bits.

Padding MAY be included on outgoing packets as specified in the ESP document.

The RFC also compares ESP_NULL with the Authentication Header (AH). AH covers the data portion of a packet and the immutable-in-transit parts of the IP header. ESP_NULL does not include the IP header in the authentication data, which can be useful for providing IPsec services through non-IP network devices. How to do that is outside the scope of the document.
sections.eli5: The rules say the pretend lock has no key and no extra number to send. That way every computer agrees on how to handle it.

sections.title: Test Vectors
sections.content: To help build interoperable implementations, the RFC gives two test cases. In test case 1 the data is 0x123456789abcdef with a length of 8, and the output is the same value. In test case 2 the data is the 53-byte string "Network Security People Have A Strange Sense Of Humor", and the output is the identical string.
sections.eli5: The test shows that what goes in is exactly what comes out, so you can check your own copy machine works.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC is direct: NULL offers no confidentiality and no other security service. It is simply a way to represent the optional use of encryption within ESP, so that ESP can give authentication and integrity without confidentiality. Unlike AH, these services are not applied to any part of the IP header.

At the time of writing the authors knew of no evidence that ESP_NULL is any less secure than AH when using the same authentication algorithm. As ESP itself states, an ESP SA must specify at least one cryptographically strong encryption algorithm or one cryptographically strong authentication algorithm, or one of each. Finally, the authors knew of no laws preventing export of NULL with a zero-bit key length.
sections.eli5: A glass envelope hides nothing, so never use it alone. You still need a real seal, which is the authentication part, to be safe.
